doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Philadelphia clubs and writing to Nesuhi Ertegun at Atlantic from age 14
summary: As a DJ Dorn got into Philadelphia clubs free while plotting to become a producer. He wrote Atlantic's Nesuhi Ertegun from age 14 until he was hired.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: And did you go to those?

Oh are you kidding? I lived in those places. First of all, because I was on the air I could go to any club I wanted to and I didn’t have to pay, you know and that was a big deal then even though it was two dollars on the door — you know when Miles came to town it was three. It was like that. But I was also plotting and scheming. I mean I was a disc jockey, and I always wanted to be a disc jockey, but I always wanted to be a record producer. So I would go in there and I would, aside from getting all the records for free which is one of the bonuses of being a disc jockey, you get a chance to go to the clubs and hear people. And I had started writing Atlantic Records when I was 14 because I fell in love with Ray Charles and Nesuhi Ertegun was the head of the jazz division of Atlantic. I could have written to Ahmet Ertegun, I could have written to Jerry Wexler, but I happened to write to Nesuhi Ertegun. And from the age of 14 until I was 25, including the six years I was on the air, all I did was annoy them. I said I want to be a record

producer, I think I annoyed myself into a job. I produced some stuff independently that they put out, but that’s where I wanted to work was Atlantic Records. And what was your question because I’m leading towards something and now I got lost in my own nonsense.
